Kosow Lacki Old Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Kosów Lacki, Poland

Not demolished. Kosów Lacki, first recorded in 1417 and granted town-like rights in 1778, likely saw Jewish settlement (and its first synagogue and cemetery) from the late 17th century; by 1827, Jews made up 100% of the town's small population, still over 90% into the 20th century (1,316 of 1,362 residents by 1921). At the end of 1939, Germans designated the town an open ghetto ('Judenstadt'), imprisoning Jews from Mława, Wyszków, and Kalisz there too; a closed ghetto formed by spring 1941, with some residents forced into labor at the nearby Treblinka I camp. The ghetto's liquidation began September 22, 1942, sending most residents to Treblinka II. This older cemetery was destroyed during the war, its tombstones used to harden the notorious 'Black Road' leading into Treblinka; several matzevot fragments excavated from the former camp site, now displayed at the Treblinka Museum, likely originated here.
